tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size stays on that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane) until you call this tool again with preset "desktop", so reset it once you are done testing. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent, 5 touch points, and mouse-to-touch translation (hover stops producing hover states). Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

Orca-side flags are defined in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectState.hpp:16`. [OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:46](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:46) maps them to JusPrin's names:

content.text:
Each flag says roughly what kind of thing just changed in the open project. OrcaSlicer can set several at once, and the timeline joins them with "+", so `contents+plates+history` means three kinds of change happened together.

- **Selection**: what you have selected changed, such as clicking a different object. The model itself stays the same, so this never adds a timeline row.
- **Contents** (called "Objects" inside Orca): the set of objects changed. One was added, deleted, duplicated, split or renamed.
- **Transform**: an object was moved, rotated or scaled.
- **Plates**: something about the build plates changed. It covers several unrelated things:
  - a plate was added, deleted or reordered
  - a different plate became the active one
  - which plate an object sits on changed
  - slicing started, finished, or its result was thrown away because something changed
- **History**: the undo/redo list changed. Usually a new undo step was recorded, or undo or redo just became available or unavailable. It's a side effect of other changes, not a change of its own.
- **Project**: a different project is now open, such as File → New or opening a file. Instead of adding a row, this starts a fresh timeline.
- **Settings**: a print, filament or printer setting changed, such as layer height. This doesn't add a timeline row today.

Only **contents**, **transform** and **plates** add a row to the timeline. The other flags are shown only when they arrive together with one of those three.

That's why "plates" is the confusing one in your screenshot. A row that says only `(plates)` usually means slicing started or finished, not that you touched a plate.

content.text:
For moves, rotations and scaling, yes. For plates, no. The one plate change with no undo step is slicing.

**Transform (move, rotate, scale):** Orca always records an undo step for these. The only place that sends Transform passes History with it every time ([Plater.cpp:5172](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:5172)).

**Plates:** it depends on the cause.
- **Plate edits you make**, like adding, deleting, switching or reordering plates, do record an undo step. For example, `take_snapshot("add partplate")` at [Plater.cpp:10142](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:10142) and `take_snapshot("select partplate!")` at [Plater.cpp:17668](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:17668). Those calls send Plates and History together.
- **Slicing starting, finishing or being thrown away** also sends Plates, but it isn't an undo step, so History isn't set ([OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:197](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:197)). That's why some rows in your screenshot say only `(plates)`.

The reverse doesn't hold either. History can arrive without Transform or Plates, for example when Orca records an undo step for a change that none of the other flags describe.

In the row labels, History adds almost nothing. When it appears next to contents, transform or plates, it just repeats "this was an undo-able edit." The label code ([ProjectPersistence.cpp:100](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectPersistence.cpp:100)) could leave it out. Its only other use is the Agent's approval check ([ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:23](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:23)). That check treats any project change as a reason to re-check an Agent action that's waiting for approval.

**What "timeline" means:** the list of "Project start" and "Project changed (…)" rows in the Agent panel in your screenshot. Each row is a saved copy of the project taken right after a change, and "Revert here" puts the project back to that copy. The code calls these "revisions". They're stored with the project by [ProjectPersistence.cpp](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectPersistence.cpp), separately from Orca's own undo list.

same worktree branch as Phase 3.

     loops) mid-operation** — so never adopt based on event timing.

     `auxiliary_data_dir()` != attached dir → adopt what's there; a

     `save_project_choise` is set (harness fixture sets "no").

     copies kept checkpoints to scratch before restoring.

  restore ~0.8–0.9 s, ~31 KB/checkpoint, save 220 KB/~180 ms. Re-benchmark

  2026-08-30 at Kenny's request — recover from git history or the phase

content.text:
# A cleaner rule for what goes into the Agent panel's revision timeline

**Proposal:** only create a timeline row when the inputs to the printed result actually changed. Answer that from two sources Orca already maintains: its undo list, plus a small fingerprint of the few print inputs the undo list doesn't cover. Stop inferring it from the change notifications the fork added to OrcaSlicer. Those notifications are the cause of both problems in your screenshot: they record noise (slicing, switching plates) and miss most real edits (mirror, painting, arrange, per-object settings, and more).

## What the timeline is supposed to hold

The spec already defines this ([agent-webview-bridge-handoff.md:271](agent-docs/jusprin/agent-webview-bridge-handoff.md:271)):

> Create a revision after each completed manufacturing change.

It lists geometry, transforms, plates, arrangement, modifiers, painting, settings and custom G-code as manufacturing changes. It lists messages, camera, selection and renaming as not. Slicing is a separate record the spec calls a "build".

Each row costs about 170 ms (the checkpoint is a full project file export) and about 31 KB on disk. "Revert here" permanently deletes everything after the row, including chat messages. So every noise row is a destructive button that means nothing, and every missing row is a point you can't go back to.

## What it holds today

**Noise: rows that aren't changes**
- Slicing starting, finishing, or its result being thrown away creates a `(plates)` row.
- Switching the active plate creates a `(plates+history)` row. "Slice all" switches plates itself, so one click can add several rows.

**Gaps: real edits that create no row**

I had a subagent trace about 30 kinds of edits through the code. I spot-checked mirror and arrange myself. These reach no notification that creates a row:
- Transforms: mirror, arrange, orient, fill bed, moving the wipe tower
- Painting: supports, seams, color, fuzzy skin, brim ears
- Parts: adding a modifier or part, changing a part's type, split to parts
- Per-object settings: settings overrides, filament assignment, layer ranges, variable layer height
- Plates: the plate settings dialog (bed type, print order), locking a plate
- Other: custom G-code from the preview slider, text/emboss/SVG, adding a primitive, toggling printable, reload from disk
- Print, filament and printer settings (by design today)

Many of these do produce a row by accident. If the plate had been sliced, the edit throws the slice away, and that shows up as `(plates)`. On an unsliced plate the edit leaves no row at all.

**Labels:** `contents+plates+history` describes which code ran, not what you did.

## Why patching the flags won't fix it

The decision rests on about 20 notification calls placed by hand in OrcaSlicer code. They answer "which code path ran", not "did the print's inputs change". Closing the gaps would mean adding calls in 20 or more more places in Orca files. Each one is another rebase conflict for the fork, and every future Orca feature would silently become a new gap.

## The proposal

**1. Decide from state, not from events.** A row is created when either of these is true:
- **Orca recorded a real undo step since the last row.** Orca already defines "real" in `src/slic3r/Utils/UndoRedo.hpp:100`: an Action or tool-action undo step whose name doesn't end in "!". Orca names selection steps and plate switching with a trailing "!" (`"select partplate!"`), and slicing never records an undo step. Orca uses this same rule for its unsaved-changes asterisk and auto-backup, so it's maintained upstream. It covers every undo-able edit in the gap list, including undo and redo themselves.
- **The inputs Orca keeps outside the undo list changed.** These are the print/filament/printer settings in force (including unsaved edits), the per-plate settings, and the per-plate custom G-code. A small fingerprint of these, compared with the last row's, covers settings, the plate settings dialog and the preview slider.

**2. Check at a quiet moment, not inside each event.** Run the check when the app goes idle after activity, so a burst of changes gives one row. Don't check while a tool like paint or cut is open, or while a background job like arrange is running. When the tool closes or the job ends, one row captures the whole session. This mirrors how Orca already merges a painting session into one undo step.

**3. Labels come from Orca's undo-step names.** Examples: "Move Object", "Arrange", "Variable layer height - Smooth all". A few are internal names ("select_arrange partplate", "smooth_mesh") and need a small table of friendlier names. Settings rows use the setting's own label, which the adapter already computes for the "N changes from preset" line on the setup card.

**4. Where the code lives.** The check goes in `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter`, which is JusPrin code. It publishes one new change reason, "manufacturing change", together with the label. `ProjectPersistence` creates a row only when it sees that reason. The flag-joining code (`kManufacturingReasons`, `cause_of`) is deleted.

It needs no OrcaSlicer file changes. Plater already exposes `undo_redo_stack_main()` (Plater.hpp:597), and the gizmo state is readable through `canvas3D()`. The existing 20 notification calls stay, because the Agent page's live context still depends on them.

## What you'd see

| Action | Today | Proposed |
|---|---|---|
| Move, rotate or scale | row | row |
| Mirror, arrange, paint, add modifier | usually no row | row (painting: one per session) |
| Change layer height | row only if the plate was sliced | row |
| Slice, or slice all | one or more rows | no row |
| Switch plate, select object | row / no row | no row |
| Undo | row | row, labeled with what was undone |

## Alternatives I rejected

- **Add the missing notification calls and split "plates" into plate layout vs active plate.** This is the fork-maintenance cost described above, and it never stays complete.
- **Use the slicer's own "did the inputs change" answer (`background_process.apply()`).** It only examines the plate currently being sliced, so edits on other plates are invisible.
- **Compare full project exports.** At about 170 ms each, that's fine for saving a checkpoint but too slow to run as the "did anything change" check.

## Related problem, same cause

The Agent's approval-staleness check ([ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:22](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:22)) relies on the same notifications. If you approve an Agent proposal after mirroring or painting, it won't be flagged as out of date. The new "manufacturing change" reason could feed that check too.

## Open questions for you

1. **Renames.** Orca treats renaming an object or plate as an edit; the spec says renaming creates no row. I'd follow the spec and filter renames out, unless object names matter to the printer. I haven't checked whether they end up in the G-code.
2. **Settings edits in a row.** Should several settings changes with nothing else in between merge into one row? I'd merge them, so tuning five settings doesn't add five Revert buttons.
3. **Unverified:** whether increasing or decreasing instance counts records an undo step. If it doesn't, it goes into the fingerprint too.

content.text:
OrcaSlicer keeps settings in three places: named presets saved as files in its data folder, unsaved edits held only in memory, and a full copy inside each saved project file. "Settings in force" means the values the slicer would use if you sliced right now: your selected presets plus any unsaved edits on top. Saving a preset writes it to disk for use in other projects; saving the project copies whatever is in force into the .3mf.

## Where settings live

1. **Named presets** (print, filament, printer) are files in OrcaSlicer's data folder:
   - Built-in presets: `<data folder>/system/`.
   - Your own: `<data folder>/user/<folder>/process/`, `.../filament/` and `.../machine/`. `<folder>` is `default` when you're not signed in and your account's folder when you are (`PresetBundle.cpp:1575-1584`; folder names in `Preset.hpp:20-24`).
   - For stock OrcaSlicer on a Mac the data folder is `~/Library/Application Support/OrcaSlicer`. I haven't checked whether JusPrin's rebrand renames it.
2. **Unsaved edits.** Changing a value in the settings tab doesn't write any file. The preset is shown as modified, and the new value exists only in memory.
3. **The project file.** Saving a project writes the full set of settings in force, unsaved edits included, into the .3mf as `Metadata/project_settings.config`. The code uses `full_config_secure()` (Plater.cpp:15728), which removes only printer connection details such as host, API key and password (`PresetBundle.cpp:3865`).

## What "settings in force" means

It's the answer to "what would the slicer use right now". That's the selected print, filament and printer presets, with your unsaved edits on top, plus a few project-level values such as filament colors. In code it's `preset_bundle->full_config()`.

This is why my proposal fingerprints the settings in force rather than tracking preset names. An unsaved edit changes the print without touching any preset file, and saving a preset changes a file without changing the print.

## How to save settings in OrcaSlicer

- **Save the preset.** Click the save icon in the settings tab. The Save Preset dialog asks for a name and offers two choices (`SavePresetDialog.cpp:108-109`):
  - **User Preset** is available in every project.
  - **Preset Inside Project** belongs to this project only.

  Some presets also show a **Detach from parent** checkbox, which cuts the link to the built-in preset the new one was based on.
- **Answer the prompt when switching presets.** If you pick another preset while the current one has unsaved edits, Orca asks you to "Transfer or discard changes":
  - **Transfer** carries your edits over to the newly chosen preset.
  - **Discard** (labeled "Don't save" in some cases) throws them away.
  - **Save** saves them as a preset first.
- **Save the project.** Your edits go into the .3mf even if you never saved a preset.

## What happens when you save

- **As a User Preset:**
  - The preset is written as a file in your user folder.
  - It becomes the selected preset, the modified marker clears, and it appears in the dropdowns in every project.
  - The settings in force don't change, because the values are the same; they now just have a name.
  - It's flagged for the app's background preset sync (`Tab.cpp:6727-6739`), which uploads it to your account when you're signed in. I didn't trace which service that sync talks to.
  - The save call passes the parent preset's config (`Preset.cpp` around line 2978). I believe that means the file stores only the values that differ from the parent, but I didn't read the save function to confirm.
- **As a Preset Inside Project:** the preset is marked as belonging to the project (`Preset.cpp` around line 2947). Saving the project then embeds it in the .3mf (`get_current_project_embedded_presets()`, Plater.cpp:15825).
- **When the project is opened later**, Orca looks for a preset with the same name:
  - If it finds one with identical values, it selects it.
  - If the values differ, it selects that preset and applies the project's values as unsaved edits, so the differences show in the settings tab (`Preset.cpp:2601-2607`).
  - If no preset has that name, it loads the project's settings as a separate preset.

**What this means for the timeline proposal:** saving a preset changes nothing about the print, so it shouldn't add a timeline row. Editing a value or switching to a preset with different values should.

content.text:
Project saving is triggered from the File menu, a keyboard shortcut, Orca's top-bar save button, or the "save before continuing?" prompt. It has no button in the settings tab, and the JusPrin shell's own header has no Save item.

**What saves the project:**
- **File → Save Project**, shortcut Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac). File → Save Project as… is Ctrl+Shift+S (Cmd+Shift+S). Code: `MainFrame.cpp:2730-2745`; the shortcuts are also handled directly at `MainFrame.cpp:726-727`.
- **The save button in Orca's top bar.** Its handler calls `save_project()` (`BBLTopbar.cpp:417-421`). I found no JusPrin shell code that hides this bar. I believe it only appears on Windows and Linux, since macOS uses the system menu bar, but I haven't checked that.
- **The "The current project has unsaved changes, save it before continue?" prompt** (`Plater.cpp:14732`). It appears when you start a new project, open another project, or quit the app with unsaved changes (`Plater.cpp:12078` in `new_project`, `:12157` in `load_project`, `MainFrame.cpp:600` on close). Choosing Yes runs the same save. If you tick "Remember my choice", Orca stops asking and always saves or always discards.

**JusPrin's own header:** the "…" menu (`StatusRow.cpp:547-555`) only has the project summary, Project details, Back to Prepare, and Preferences. There's no Save there, so in the new UI you save through the File menu, the shortcut, or the prompt.

**What a project save writes**, into one .3mf file:
- the objects and plates
- the full settings in force, including unsaved preset edits, in `Metadata/project_settings.config`
- any presets you saved as "Preset Inside Project"
- JusPrin's Agent conversations and revision checkpoints, stored under `Auxiliaries/JusPrin/`

It also clears Orca's unsaved-changes marker. It does not change any preset file, so the preset still shows as modified.

**The two saves are independent:**

| | Saving a preset (settings tab icon) | Saving the project (File → Save Project) |
|---|---|---|
| Writes | one preset file in your user folder | the .3mf project file |
| Unsaved edits end up | in the preset, available to every project | in the project only; the preset still shows as modified |
| Clears | the preset's modified marker | the project's unsaved-changes marker |

content.text:
That's right, you can't save over a system preset. The Save Preset dialog refuses: if you type an existing system preset's name, it shows "Overwriting a system profile is not allowed." and won't let you continue (`SavePresetDialog.cpp:164-167`).

The rule is in `Preset::can_overwrite()` (`Preset.hpp:247`). You can't overwrite a preset if it is:
- a **system** preset that ships with the app (the `system/` folder),
- one of Orca's built-in **default** presets,
- a preset that came from an installed **config bundle**.

When you save changes to a system preset, the dialog suggests a new name such as "0.20mm Standard @BBL X1C - Copy" (`SavePresetDialog.cpp:39` and `:277`). Saving creates a new preset of your own, and the system preset stays unchanged.

You have two places to save it, not just one:
- **User Preset:** a file in your user folder, available in every project.
- **Preset Inside Project:** stored with the project and saved into its .3mf.

Either way, the new preset keeps a link to the system preset it came from, so it can pick up updates to values you didn't change. The **Detach from parent** checkbox, when shown, breaks that link.

content.text:
Not quite. The project doesn't store your presets plus a separate list of unsaved edits. It stores one flattened copy of every setting value in force, labeled with which presets were selected and which values differ from them. Only presets you saved as "Preset Inside Project" are stored whole.

## Settings in the project file

**1. `Metadata/project_settings.config`: the flattened settings.** It contains:
- **Every value in force:** print, each filament, and printer, with unsaved edits already applied. Nothing marks which values are unsaved edits. Printer connection details (host, API key, password) are removed first (`PresetBundle.cpp:3865`).
- **The names of the selected presets:** `print_settings_id`, `filament_settings_id` (one per filament slot) and `printer_settings_id` (`PresetBundle.cpp:4138-4140`).
- **Each one's system parent** (`inherits_group`), meaning the built-in preset it was based on.
- **A list of which settings differ from that system parent** (`different_settings_to_system`), one entry for the process, one per filament, and one for the printer (`PresetBundle.cpp:3928`, `:4160`).

That list compares the current values with the **system** preset, not with your saved preset. If you selected a user preset and then edited it, the user preset's own changes and your unsaved edits end up in the same list, and nothing tells them apart. I'm reading that from the code, not from a test.

**2. Whole presets, only for "Preset Inside Project".** Every preset marked as belonging to the project is written as its own file, whether or not it's currently selected (`Preset.cpp:1993-2005`). The files are `Metadata/print_setting_N`, `filament_settings_N` and `machine_settings_N` (`bbs_3mf.cpp:222-225`).

**Not included:** your ordinary User Presets. The project only records their names, plus the flattened values.

That's why opening the project on another computer still works. If no preset with that name exists there, Orca turns the project's values into a separate preset. If one does exist but its values differ, Orca selects it and shows the differences as unsaved edits.

## Other settings-like data in the file

Per-object and per-plate settings are stored separately from the presets (`bbs_3mf.cpp:209-226`):

| File | Contains |
|---|---|
| `Metadata/model_settings.config` | per-object setting overrides, and plate settings such as bed type, print order and plate name |
| `Metadata/layer_heights_profile.txt` | variable layer height |
| `Metadata/layer_config_ranges.xml` | layer-range modifiers |
| `Metadata/custom_gcode_per_layer.xml` | color changes, pauses and custom G-code from the preview slider |
| `Metadata/filament_sequence.json`, `brim_ear_points.txt`, `cut_information.xml` | filament order, brim ears, cut connectors |

JusPrin's Agent conversations and revision checkpoints sit under `Auxiliaries/JusPrin/`. The objects themselves, including painted surfaces, are in the 3D model files. I believe painting is stored with the mesh, but I didn't trace that part.
